title: Week 4 · Parts of speech and named entities

lines: Now we label every single word, not the whole text.
Part of speech tagging gives each word its grammar role: noun, verb, adjective.
Book that flight: here book is a verb.
Hand me that book: here book is a noun. The context decides.
Only a few words can have more than one tag.
But they are very common words, like that, back and book.
So in real text, most of the words we read are ambiguous.
A simple baseline always picks the most frequent tag. It is often right, but it gets book that flight wrong.
Named entity recognition finds names in the text, and their type.
It has two jobs. First, where does the name start and end? San Francisco is two words, but one name.
Second, what type is it? Washington can be a person, a city, or a government.
To label names word by word, we use B I O.
B means begin. I means inside the same name. O means outside.
San is B location. Francisco is I location. Every other word is O.
The same word can have different tags. The context decides.
Named entity recognition is harder than part of speech tagging: it needs the boundaries and the type.
And B I O turns names into one label per word.
